output.title: What name handling hides in a small business workflow
output.body:
What name handling hides is usually not philosophical. It is a workflow choice: do you treat name variants as the same person, or do you handle each variant separately until a human checks it?

For a 1–10 person business, that choice matters only if names affect routing, follow-up, or handoff. If a lead arrives as “John Smith” in one form and “J. Smith” in another, the issue is not the name itself. The issue is whether the inconsistency creates a duplicate record, a missed reply, or a messy handoff between inbox, CRM, and invoice work. If it does not change the work, it is noise.

The practical next step is simple: pick one recurring place where names enter your process, such as a form, inbox thread, or CRM field, and review 10–20 recent examples. Look for the same person appearing in more than one format, or different people being forced into one format. That tells you whether you need name matching, stricter intake rules, or no automation at all.

If money movement is involved, keep human approval in the loop. That is still the sane part of the system.
